title: Iron Bends, Steel Holds: Interstitial Compounds and Alloys
subject: Chemistry
objective: Pure iron bends because layers of atoms slide over each other; less than 2 % carbon in the gaps locks the layers and gives hard steel. Interstitial compounds form when small atoms such as H, C or N are trapped in a metal lattice (TiC, Mn₄N, Fe₃H, VH₀.₅₆, TiH₁.₇): non-stoichiometric, very hard, higher melting than the pure metal, still conducting and chemically inert. Alloys form when atoms of similar size (metallic radii within about 15 %, e.g. Fe 126 and Cr 129 pm) are distributed randomly among each other: stainless steel, brass (Cu–Zn) and bronze (Cu–Sn), hard and often high melting.

short.q: What are interstitial compounds? Give two examples.
short.solution: Compounds formed when small atoms like H, C or N are trapped inside the crystal lattices of metals; usually non-stoichiometric. Examples: TiC, Mn₄N (also Fe₃H, VH₀.₅₆, TiH₁.₇).

short.q: State four properties of interstitial compounds.
short.solution: High melting points, higher than pure metals; very hard (some borides approach diamond); retain metallic conductivity; chemically inert.

short.q: Why do transition metals form alloys readily?
short.solution: Their metallic radii are similar (within about 15 %), so atoms of one metal can be distributed randomly among the atoms of the other in a solid solution; the alloys are hard and often high melting.
